Question: Is the inability to create relations, even with therapists, a cognitive deficit or personality deficit?
Answer: Believing that you are unable to create relationships may be a cognitive issue or a schema you have developed. You may refer to the fact that you face significant challenges in forming and maintaining relationships, but that doesn't mean you are incapable of doing it. It is not accurate to describe facing challenges in forming relationships as "an inability," even for neurodivergent people or individuals on the autism spectrum. Yes, it's true that many people find it very challenging to develop a relationship with another person because they suffer from social anxiety or have attachment issues that make them either too needy or too detached, or because they lack social skills and suffer from a lack of trust, etc. Still, that doesn't mean they would never be able to form a relationship. It's obvious, though, that past experiences, traumatic circumstances, or unresolved emotional issues can significantly affect our ability to form relationships. If someone had a relationship that hurt them badly, they may be afraid to be in another relationship because they want to avoid getting hurt again. It's also possible to suffer from a specific emotional issue that has, as a characteristic, the difficulty to socialize or engage socially. These could be personality traits such as: There are also more severe reasons to have difficulty forming relationships. People suffering from personality disorders may have this difficulty as part of their symptoms. For example, for BPD, maintaining relationships is by definition difficult because of high dependency, frequent conflicts rooted in feeling rejected, criticized, or abandoned. The idealization and devaluation are also on the way to seeing the person as a constant source, which breaks the relationship. People with schizoid personality disorder avoid social activities and interacting with others, don't desire or enjoy close relationships, even with family, and prefer to be alone. Why? From what we have learned lately, it may be based on trauma and the fear of people. Like with many other syndromes, the person who suffered an emotional injury adapts to the best of their possibilities to surviving without taking chances to get injured again. Many times that means isolating and avoiding people. But it’s always possible to overcome the challenges, to learn social skills, and to dare to find some connection. We are social beings and we need each other. Isolation is not good for our health.

Question: Can someone have BPD and be narcissistic?
Answer: I have still not met a person with BPD (pwBPD) without narcissistic traits. So, yes, individuals with BPD can exhibit narcissistic traits. However, this is different from meeting the criteria for both disorders. Narcissistic traits include a sense of entitlement, sensitivity to criticism, manipulative and exploitative behaviors, unstable relationships, a need for admiration, attention-seeking, arrogance, envy, a need to control, superficiality, fragile self-esteem, and exaggeration of achievements. Don’t you think that almost everyone has, to some extent, narcissistic traits? Who doesn’t like to be admired, or experience envy, or feel entitled to something? That’s even more pronounced in this era where everyone wants (and can) be famous overnight! Also, be proud of one’s achievements is something we normally judge as narcissistic. It’s hard to win with all the terms and judgments assigned to people that behave a little off from our expectations. That’s actually unfair! On the other hand, saying that someone with a personality disorder is not narcissistic is almost an oxymoron. Question: Is it normal to form imaginary relationships because of stress disorders like PTSD and depression?
Answer: Let me start by clarifying what “normal” means. Normal is what a lot of people do in the same way. That many people do things the same way doesn’t not mean they are right or wrong. We may have the tendency to equate “abnormal” with wrong, but that’s not the case. So, I wonder if you are asking about having imaginary relationships to be common, or wrong. I don’t think it’s very common, but it is definitely not wrong. When someone is struggling emotionally with feelings like depression or loneliness, it becomes necessary to find strategies to feel less bad. That’s common. The type of strategies vary a lot. Imagination is a very powerful tool that can bring aliviation to emotional distress. Daydreaming, fantasizing, and imagination are typical cognitive processes that people engage in to varying degrees. These activities are a normal part of human thinking and can serve various purposes, such as problem-solving, creativity, and entertainment. Imaginary relationships could be helpful as long as they don’t become the only way to relate and they are not a substitute for real-life social connections. An excessive focus on imaginary relationships can lead to social isolation; excessive reliance on fantasy relationships may hinder individuals from addressing the underlying issues and can delay or impede the individual's progress in seeking treatment and support for their mental health issues. if someone is experiencing excessive and distressing daydreams and everything in life moves around the imaginary relationships to the point where it significantly impairs their daily functioning and their ability to distinguish between their inner world and external reality, it could be a sign of a different mental health concern, such as a dissociative disorder or other conditions. What distinguishes the healthy from the unhealthy are the consequences into being functioning or becoming dysfunctional and impairing.

Question: What happens if trauma is not resolved?
Answer: If you were exposed to toxic stress for a long period of time, then the consequences will also last long and they can become a hindrance in your life. If the stress/risk/threat that caused the trauma was only one event, then the symptoms will disappear slowly but certainly. It will also depend on your level of resilience, and/or the way you deal with adversity. If you tend to worry a lot, or are normally fearful, you could stay traumatized for years. Many individuals “learn” to live with the disorder —whether PTSD or C-PTSD— and could have very functional lives even when they carry the burden of a system that is never well regulated, and therefore, never works in optimal conditions. That could appear as emotionality (emotional dysregulation), as disengagement and emotional numbness, as physical problems, or a combination of them. We were not aware of the phenomenon of trauma until relatively recent (the 1980s). People had no idea what was happening to them for decades, and all sorts of diagnoses were given to traumatized people, making them feel defective, mentally ill, depressed, anxious, bipolar, and so on. Those people either were medicated without much improvement, or learned to rely on being numbed by either legal or illegal drugs, alcohol, or emotionally draining relationships. Most of the time, people will not even give attention to their symptoms and just assume there was something wrong with them, and therefore, not deserving much. What I mean is that people can live with trauma for a very long time without clear dysfunction, but at some point, the system breaks, and many problems arise. Reading your question again, it may be the case that you are using the term “trauma” to refer to the situation and not to the disorder. In that case, if the traumatizing situation doesn’t end, the person just keeps getting sicker and sicker, and their nervous system gets more and more dysregulated. There is no healing of trauma (PTSD or C-PTSD) until the traumatic stress and the dangerous circumstances disappear.
